Exercises

Problems to check your understanding of this chapter. The solutions are folded away — try them yourself first.

Easy

1Easy

Let fff be continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), with ∣f′(x)∣≤M\lvert f'(x) \rvert \le M∣f′(x)∣≤M for all x∈(a,b)x \in (a,b)x∈(a,b) and some constant M≥0M \ge 0M≥0.

Prove the inequality below for all x,y∈[a,b]x, y \in [a,b]x,y∈[a,b]. (Hence fff is uniformly continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b].)

∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤M∣x−y∣\lvert f(x) - f(y) \rvert \le M\lvert x - y \rvert∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤M∣x−y∣
  • The Secant Meets Its Parallel Tangent
  • Differentiable Implies Continuous
Show solution

  1. The case x=yx = yx=y is trivial, so let x<yx < yx<y. Since fff is continuous on [x,y]⊂[a,b][x,y] \subset [a,b][x,y]⊂[a,b] and differentiable on (x,y)⊂(a,b)(x,y) \subset (a,b)(x,y)⊂(a,b), the Mean Value Theorem applies on [x,y][x,y][x,y]: for some c∈(x,y)c \in (x,y)c∈(x,y), f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x)f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x)f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x).

  2. Taking absolute values, ∣f(y)−f(x)∣=∣f′(c)∣⋅∣y−x∣≤M∣y−x∣\lvert f(y) - f(x) \rvert = \lvert f'(c) \rvert \cdot \lvert y - x \rvert \le M\lvert y - x \rvert∣f(y)−f(x)∣=∣f′(c)∣⋅∣y−x∣≤M∣y−x∣. The case x>yx > yx>y is the same with the roles swapped, so the inequality holds for all x,y∈[a,b]x, y \in [a,b]x,y∈[a,b].

    This is the Lipschitz condition, and uniform continuity follows with δ=ε/M\delta = \varepsilon / Mδ=ε/M (any δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 if M=0M = 0M=0).

3Easy

Prove via the triangle inequality that f(x)=∣x∣f(x) = \lvert x \rvertf(x)=∣x∣ is convex on R\mathbb{R}R, and cite the continuity theorem for convex functions to conclude fff is continuous.

Show fff is not differentiable at 000, confirming that convexity does not imply differentiability.

∣tx+(1−t)y∣≤t∣x∣+(1−t)∣y∣(0≤t≤1)\lvert tx + (1-t)y \rvert \le t\lvert x \rvert + (1-t)\lvert y \rvert \qquad (0 \le t \le 1)∣tx+(1−t)y∣≤t∣x∣+(1−t)∣y∣(0≤t≤1)
  • Convex Functions
Show solution

  1. For 0≤t≤10 \le t \le 10≤t≤1 and x,y∈Rx, y \in \mathbb{R}x,y∈R, the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the absolute value give ∣tx+(1−t)y∣≤∣tx∣+∣(1−t)y∣=t∣x∣+(1−t)∣y∣\lvert tx + (1-t)y \rvert \le \lvert tx \rvert + \lvert (1-t)y \rvert = t\lvert x \rvert + (1-t)\lvert y \rvert∣tx+(1−t)y∣≤∣tx∣+∣(1−t)y∣=t∣x∣+(1−t)∣y∣. This is exactly the definition of convexity, so fff is convex on R\mathbb{R}R.

    A convex function is continuous on every open interval (the theorem of the convex scene), so fff is continuous everywhere.

  2. But the difference quotient at 000 is given by the formula below, which has no limit. Hence fff is not differentiable at 000 — the simplest example of a function that is convex and continuous but not differentiable.

    f(h)−f(0)h=∣h∣h={1h>0−1h<0\dfrac{f(h) - f(0)}{h} = \dfrac{\lvert h \rvert}{h} = \begin{cases} 1 & h > 0 \\ -1 & h < 0 \end{cases}hf(h)−f(0)​=h∣h∣​={1−1​h>0h<0​

Medium

4Medium

Let fff be differentiable on [a,b][a,b][a,b] with f′(x)≠0f'(x) \ne 0f′(x)=0 for every x∈[a,b]x \in [a,b]x∈[a,b].

Combining Darboux's theorem with the Mean Value Theorem, prove that fff is strictly monotone on [a,b][a,b][a,b].

  • Darboux's Theorem
  • The Secant Meets Its Parallel Tangent
Show solution

  1. By Darboux's theorem, f′f'f′ has the intermediate value property. Suppose f′f'f′ changed sign: there exist u,v∈[a,b]u, v \in [a,b]u,v∈[a,b] with f′(u)>0>f′(v)f'(u) > 0 > f'(v)f′(u)>0>f′(v).

    Applying Darboux's theorem on the interval between uuu and vvv would produce a point ccc with f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence f′f'f′ cannot change sign, and since it never vanishes, it is either everywhere positive or everywhere negative on [a,b][a,b][a,b].

  2. Consider the case f′>0f' > 0f′>0 (the negative case differs only in sign). For x<yx < yx<y, the Mean Value Theorem gives c∈(x,y)c \in (x,y)c∈(x,y) with f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x)f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x)f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x); since f′(c)>0f'(c) > 0f′(c)>0, we get f(y)>f(x)f(y) > f(x)f(y)>f(x).

    So fff is strictly increasing. Likewise f′<0f' < 0f′<0 makes fff strictly decreasing.

5Medium

Let fff be n+1n+1n+1 times continuously differentiable on [a,b][a,b][a,b] (n≥0n \ge 0n≥0).

For a≤x≤ba \le x \le ba≤x≤b, prove Taylor's formula with integral remainder \[f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k + R_n(x), \qquad R_n(x) = \frac{1}{n!}\int_a^x (x-t)^n f^{(n+1)}(t)\,dt.\]

The case n=0n = 0n=0 is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; for the induction step apply integration by parts once.

  • Taylor's Theorem: The Remainder Envelope
  • Polynomials Hugging the Curve
Show solution

  1. For n=0n = 0n=0 the formula is f(x)=f(a)+∫axf′(t) dtf(x) = f(a) + \int_a^x f'(t)\,dtf(x)=f(a)+∫ax​f′(t)dt, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. As the induction hypothesis, assume the formula for nnn holds for Cn+1C^{n+1}Cn+1 functions.

    For g∈Cn+2g \in C^{n+2}g∈Cn+2, applying it to ggg gives g(x)=Tn(x)+1n!∫ax(x−t)ng(n+1)(t) dtg(x) = T_n(x) + \frac{1}{n!}\int_a^x (x-t)^n g^{(n+1)}(t)\,dtg(x)=Tn​(x)+n!1​∫ax​(x−t)ng(n+1)(t)dt, where TnT_nTn​ is the degree-nnn Taylor polynomial.

  2. Apply integration by parts to the remainder integral: with u=g(n+1)(t)u = g^{(n+1)}(t)u=g(n+1)(t) and dv=(x−t)n dtdv = (x-t)^n\,dtdv=(x−t)ndt, we have du=g(n+2)(t) dtdu = g^{(n+2)}(t)\,dtdu=g(n+2)(t)dt and v=−(x−t)n+1n+1v = -\dfrac{(x-t)^{n+1}}{n+1}v=−n+1(x−t)n+1​.

    Since g(n+1)g^{(n+1)}g(n+1) and (x−t)n+1(x-t)^{n+1}(x−t)n+1 are continuous, parts is legitimate and \[\int_a^x (x-t)^n g^{(n+1)}(t)\,dt = \left[-\frac{(x-t)^{n+1}}{n+1}\,g^{(n+1)}(t)\right]_a^x + \frac{1}{n+1}\int_a^x (x-t)^{n+1} g^{(n+2)}(t)\,dt.\] The boundary term is 000 at t=xt = xt=x and gives (x−a)n+1n+1 g(n+1)(a)\dfrac{(x-a)^{n+1}}{n+1}\,g^{(n+1)}(a)n+1(x−a)n+1​g(n+1)(a) at t=at = at=a (the minus sign flips).

  3. Multiplying by 1n!\frac{1}{n!}n!1​, the remainder integral becomes g(n+1)(a)(n+1)!(x−a)n+1+1(n+1)!∫ax(x−t)n+1g(n+2)(t) dt\dfrac{g^{(n+1)}(a)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1} + \dfrac{1}{(n+1)!}\int_a^x (x-t)^{n+1} g^{(n+2)}(t)\,dt(n+1)!g(n+1)(a)​(x−a)n+1+(n+1)!1​∫ax​(x−t)n+1g(n+2)(t)dt. The first term is exactly the degree-(n+1)(n+1)(n+1) Taylor term, and the second is Rn+1(x)R_{n+1}(x)Rn+1​(x).

    Hence g(x)=Tn+1(x)+Rn+1(x)g(x) = T_{n+1}(x) + R_{n+1}(x)g(x)=Tn+1​(x)+Rn+1​(x), which is the formula for n+1n+1n+1. By induction the proof is complete for all n≥0n \ge 0n≥0.

6Medium

Consider the map T(x)=12+xT(x) = \dfrac{1}{2+x}T(x)=2+x1​ on [0,1][0,1][0,1].

(a) Show TTT maps [0,1][0,1][0,1] into itself and is a contraction with constant c=1/4c = 1/4c=1/4. (b) Cite the Banach fixed point theorem to find the unique fixed point of TTT (solve the quadratic), and explain why iteration from any starting point converges to it.

∣T(x)−T(y)∣=∣x−y∣(2+x)(2+y)≤14 ∣x−y∣\lvert T(x) - T(y) \rvert = \frac{\lvert x - y \rvert}{(2+x)(2+y)} \le \frac14\,\lvert x - y \rvert∣T(x)−T(y)∣=(2+x)(2+y)∣x−y∣​≤41​∣x−y∣
x=12+x  ⟺  x2+2x−1=0  ⟺  x=2−1≈0.4142x = \frac{1}{2+x} \iff x^2 + 2x - 1 = 0 \iff x = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.4142x=2+x1​⟺x2+2x−1=0⟺x=2​−1≈0.4142
  • The Contraction Cobweb
Show solution

  1. (a) TTT is decreasing on [0,1][0,1][0,1] with T(0)=1/2T(0) = 1/2T(0)=1/2 and T(1)=1/3T(1) = 1/3T(1)=1/3, so T([0,1])=[1/3,1/2]⊂[0,1]T([0,1]) = [1/3, 1/2] \subset [0,1]T([0,1])=[1/3,1/2]⊂[0,1].

    For x,y∈[0,1]x, y \in [0,1]x,y∈[0,1], ∣T(x)−T(y)∣=∣2+y−(2+x)(2+x)(2+y)∣=∣x−y∣(2+x)(2+y)\lvert T(x) - T(y) \rvert = \left\lvert \dfrac{2+y-(2+x)}{(2+x)(2+y)} \right\rvert = \dfrac{\lvert x - y \rvert}{(2+x)(2+y)}∣T(x)−T(y)∣=​(2+x)(2+y)2+y−(2+x)​​=(2+x)(2+y)∣x−y∣​. Since (2+x)(2+y)≥2⋅2=4(2+x)(2+y) \ge 2 \cdot 2 = 4(2+x)(2+y)≥2⋅2=4, we get ∣T(x)−T(y)∣≤14∣x−y∣\lvert T(x) - T(y) \rvert \le \dfrac14\lvert x - y \rvert∣T(x)−T(y)∣≤41​∣x−y∣ — a contraction with constant 1/41/41/4.

  2. (b) [0,1][0,1][0,1] is complete, so the Banach fixed point theorem (the Banach scene) gives TTT a unique fixed point x∗∈[0,1]x^\ast \in [0,1]x∗∈[0,1]. The equation x=12+xx = \dfrac{1}{2+x}x=2+x1​ is equivalent to x2+2x−1=0x^2 + 2x - 1 = 0x2+2x−1=0, with roots x=−1±2x = -1 \pm \sqrt{2}x=−1±2​. The only one in [0,1][0,1][0,1] is x∗=2−1≈0.4142x^\ast = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.4142x∗=2​−1≈0.4142.

    By the same theorem, the iteration xn+1=T(xn)x_{n+1} = T(x_n)xn+1​=T(xn​) from any x0∈[0,1]x_0 \in [0,1]x0​∈[0,1] converges to x∗x^\astx∗ — the error shrinks by at least a factor of 1/41/41/4 each step.
